cards.title: Somebody else does it — you only arrange it
cards.title_cz: Dělá to někdo jiný — vy to jen zařídíte
cards.body: **have** or **get** + **object** + **past participle** says that you did not do the job yourself: you paid for it, booked it, or asked for it. The English looks like a passive because it is one — the difference is that the object comes **before** the past participle.
cards.body_cz: **have** nebo **get** + **předmět** + **příčestí minulé** říká, že jste tu práci nedělali sami: zaplatili jste ji, objednali nebo o ni požádali. Angličtina vypadá jako pasivum, protože jím je — rozdíl je v tom, že předmět stojí **před** příčestím minulým.

table.caption: The tense sits in have / get
rows: She has her hair cut every month.
I am having a new kitchen installed.
I had my car repaired yesterday.
He has just had his phone repaired.
We are going to have the windows cleaned.
You should have that tooth checked.

cards.title: have or get — and the questions trap
cards.title_cz: have, nebo get — a past na otázky
cards.body: **get** is the informal one and is far more common in speech; **have** is neutral and safer in writing. Either way, both are **ordinary verbs** in this pattern, so questions and negatives need **do / did** — not the auxiliary *have* you use for the present perfect.
cards.body_cz: **get** je neformální a v mluvené řeči mnohem častější; **have** je neutrální a v psaném projevu jistější. Tak či tak jsou obě v této vazbě **plnovýznamová slovesa**, takže otázky a zápor potřebují **do / did** — ne pomocné *have*, které znáte z předpřítomného času.
points: Did you have your eyes tested? (not: Have you your eyes tested?)
We didn't get the report finished in time.
Have you had the heater fixed yet? (here the first have IS the perfect)
In speech, get wins: I got my shoes repaired.

cards.title: Naming the person changes the form
cards.title_cz: Když uvedete osobu, změní se tvar
cards.body: If you say **who** does the job, the past participle disappears. **have + person + base form** is an instruction you give. **get + person + to + infinitive** is persuasion. This is the one place the two verbs stop being interchangeable.
cards.body_cz: Když řeknete, **kdo** tu práci dělá, příčestí minulé zmizí. **have + osoba + základní tvar** je pokyn, který dáváte. **get + osoba + to + infinitiv** je přemlouvání. Právě tady přestávají být obě slovesa zaměnitelná.
points: I will have the waiter bring the menu. (base form, no to)
I got my sister to help with the cooking. (to + infinitive)
Compare: I had my car repaired. (thing — past participle)
Also for machines: I couldn't get the printer to work.

cards.title: The same words, an unwelcome meaning
cards.body: **have something done** has a second reading: something bad happened to you and you did not arrange it at all. Only the situation tells the two apart — *I had my hair cut* is a hairdresser, *I had my bike stolen* is a thief.
cards.body_cz: **have something done** má i druhé čtení: stalo se vám něco nepříjemného a vy jste to vůbec nezařizovali. Rozliší je jen situace — *I had my hair cut* je kadeřník, *I had my bike stolen* je zloděj.
points: He had his bike stolen last night. (he did not arrange it)
They had their flight cancelled. (the airline did it to them)
Czech usually says it with an impersonal plural: ukradli mu kolo
get works here too: he got his bike stolen

table.caption: Avoid / Say
rows: past participle, not the base form
have is an ordinary verb here
I will have the waiter to bring it.
I will have the waiter **bring** it.
I got my sister help me.
I got my sister **to** help me.
